claims.text: Combining in situ HTXRD with TGA enables real-time observation of phase transformations and oxidation-related mass changes.
The combined method can clarify the dynamic relationship between oxide-scale growth and phase stability at elevated temperatures.
The starting material is homogenized and initially single-phase, such as FCC or BCC.
In situ HTXRD can monitor phase evolution through changes in diffraction patterns during high-temperature oxidation.
TGA can simultaneously measure real-time mass changes caused by oxidation.
Temperatures of approximately 600–900 °C or higher in controlled oxidizing environments are appropriate conditions for the proposed measurements.
Correlating TGA mass data with diffraction peak intensities or shifts can identify evolving oxide layers and new phases.
Continuous HTXRD phase mapping can reveal emergent oxide phases and structural transformations during oxidation.
The combined measurements illuminate how elemental diffusion and structural changes influence, and are influenced by, ongoing oxidation reactions.
The time-resolved data will reveal a strong correlation between mass-gain rate and the appearance or transformation of oxide phases.
Combined TGA–HTXRD can precisely link oxidation kinetics to phase evolution in real time.
Conventional ex situ oxidation and post-exposure XRD capture only final or intermittent material states.
Ex situ methods make it difficult to track transient phase transformations and connect them with oxidation kinetics.
The proposed measurements require specialized X-ray instrumentation capable of high-temperature in situ operation.
Sample geometry, atmosphere control, and minor-phase detection limits can affect the results.
Oxygen partial pressure, temperature gradients, and geometric factors can cause measurement errors or interpretation challenges.
In situ HTXRD is a powerful tool for identifying time- and temperature-dependent phase formation or transformation during oxidation.
Comparing simultaneous in situ measurements with ex situ measurements on identical specimens can test whether salient transformation events are captured.
Failure of HTXRD phase changes to align with TGA mass changes, or discovery of missed phases by ex situ analysis, is specified as evidence against the method's reliability.
